stem: A client learning home peritoneal dialysis is preparing to connect the transfer set for an exchange. Which action best demonstrates safe aseptic technique?

options.A: Perform hand hygiene, avoid touching open connection ends, and contact the dialysis team promptly if the open system is accidentally contaminated during the exchange.
options.B: Perform hand hygiene and put on clean gloves, then touch an open connection end briefly if the gloves have not contacted any other surface during the exchange.
options.C: Put on clean gloves before setting up the exchange and perform hand hygiene after disconnecting, because gloves provide the needed barrier while connections are open.
options.D: If an open connection is accidentally contaminated, complete the exchange and contact the dialysis team only if cloudy effluent, abdominal pain, or fever develops later.

rationale: ISPD guidance emphasizes competent hand hygiene and correct exchange technique for home peritoneal dialysis. The 2022 ISPD peritonitis guideline states that clients should seek advice immediately from the dialysis team when sterility is breached during a PD exchange and identifies touch contamination of a connection during an open exchange as wet contamination. CDC guidance also states that gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene. Therefore A is correct. B permits touch contamination of an open connection. C incorrectly treats gloves as a replacement for hand hygiene before the aseptic task. D delays reporting a recognized contamination event until symptoms appear.
educational_objective: During home peritoneal dialysis exchanges, use hand hygiene and non-touch handling of open connections, and report an open-system contamination promptly rather than relying on gloves or waiting for peritonitis symptoms.
source_document_title: Teaching peritoneal dialysis: A position paper for the International Society for Peritoneal Dialysis; ISPD peritonitis guideline recommendations: 2022 update on prevention and treatment
source_version_date: ISPD teaching position paper 2025; adult peritonitis guideline 2022 with published corrigenda through 2024
source_locator: Teaching peritoneal dialysis (2025) > Methods of training/educational interventions: hand hygiene is an example of a skill that should be demonstrated with rationale and reproduced by the learner with psychomotor competence. ISPD peritonitis guideline recommendations (2022) > Prevention of peritonitis > Contamination of PD system: seek advice immediately from the treatment team if contamination during PD exchange is noted; wet contamination includes breach of aseptic technique or touch contamination of the connection during an open PD exchange.
source_claim_supported: Home PD training requires competent hand hygiene and exchange technique, and contamination of an open PD connection is a sterility breach that should be reported immediately to the dialysis team.

supporting_sources.document_title: ISPD peritonitis guideline recommendations: 2022 update on prevention and treatment
supporting_sources.version_date: First published March 10, 2022; corrigenda published 2023 and 2024
supporting_sources.locator: Prevention of peritonitis > Contamination of PD system: immediately seek treatment-team advice after contamination; wet contamination includes breach of aseptic technique or touch contamination of the connection during an open PD exchange.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Open-system touch contamination during a PD exchange is a recognized peritonitis-risk event requiring immediate advice from the dialysis team.

supporting_sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
supporting_sources.document_title: Clinical Safety: Hand Hygiene for Healthcare Workers
supporting_sources.locator: Know when to wear (and change) gloves: gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene; perform hand hygiene before donning gloves when the task requires gloves and after glove removal.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Glove use does not replace hand hygiene.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control, printed p. 24: apply principles of infection prevention, including hand hygiene, aseptic technique, isolation, sterile technique, and standard/enhanced barrier precautions; educate clients and staff regarding infection-prevention measures.
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — aseptic technique during home peritoneal dialysis exchanges
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four choices to remove the uniquely-long keyed answer and converted the distractors into realistic errors involving glove substitution, touch contamination, and delayed reporting of an open-system sterility breach. The corrected item retains the home-PD aseptic-technique construct and uses current ISPD and CDC guidance with a direct 2026 NCSBN infection-prevention locator.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Home peritoneal dialysis — aseptic exchange technique and contamination response
audit_findings.stem: PASS — specifies home PD connection setup and asks one infection-prevention action without introducing unrelated dialysis management.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — combines competent hand hygiene, non-touch handling of open connections, and prompt response to open-system contamination; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — hand hygiene and clean gloves are plausible safeguards, but touching an open connection remains a contamination event rather than an acceptable shortcut.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — gloves may be used according to local technique, but they do not replace hand hygiene before an aseptic task.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — symptoms such as cloudy effluent can indicate peritonitis, but ISPD directs immediate advice after an open-system contamination rather than waiting for symptoms.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only option that preserves aseptic technique and follows the directly cited response to contamination.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B permits touch contamination, C substitutes gloves for hand hygiene, and D delays reporting a recognized wet-contamination event.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all four options are closely matched in length and specificity; the keyed answer is not uniquely long.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Safety and Infection Prevention and Control explicitly includes hand hygiene and aseptic technique.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether clean gloves could justify touching an open connection or whether observation until symptoms develop could be reasonable; ISPD identifies open-connection touch contamination as wet contamination requiring immediate advice, and CDC states gloves do not replace hand hygiene, leaving A uniquely best.
